sections.text: An amortization calculator saves you money by letting you test changes before you make them: enter your loan, add an extra payment, and read the new payoff time and interest next to the original. On a $340,000 loan at an assumed 6.25% over 30 years, adding $150 a month cuts the term to 25 years and saves $81,011.53 of interest. This guide shows the workflow, what each result means, and how to compare scenarios fairly. For how to read the schedule row by row, see the dedicated schedule guide; this post is about using the tool.

items: Loan amount: for a new loan, the amount borrowed; for a loan in progress, your current principal balance from the latest statement.
Annual interest rate: the note rate, not the APR.
Term: choose years or months. For a loan in progress, switch to months and enter the payments you have left.
Extra monthly payment and extra annual payment: leave at zero for the baseline run.

sections.text: The baseline for the example, $340,000 at 6.25% for 360 months, is a payment of $2,093.44 and total interest of $413,637.85. In month one, interest is $340,000 x 0.0625 / 12 = $1,770.83, so only $322.61 of the payment reduces the balance. The calculator works out the payment itself, so it may differ by a few cents from the rounded figure on your statement.
Step 2: change one input at a time

rows: Extra $150 a month and $3,000 a year
One extra payment of $2,093.44 a year

sections.text: The annual amount in this calculator is applied with every twelfth payment, starting with payment 13. The savings are not additive: $150 a month alone saves $81,011.53 and $3,000 a year alone saves $112,945.97, but together they save $155,185.39, not $193,957.50, because the second source of extra money works on a balance the first has already lowered.
Step 3: compare with the alternative of a different loan

Run the same loan with a shorter term to see whether extra payments are doing something a different loan could do. A 25-year loan at 6.25% has a payment of $2,242.88 and costs $332,862.77 in interest. Paying the 30-year loan's $2,093.44 plus $150 gives $2,243.44 a month and costs $332,626.32 in interest, only $236 less. The two are almost the same, with one difference: the extra payment is voluntary. If money gets tight, you can drop back to $2,093.44, which a 25-year loan would not allow. A 20-year loan costs $391.72 more a month than the 30-year one at the same rate (payment $2,485.16) and its interest is $256,437.41. Real shorter loans may also carry different rates, so enter the rate you are quoted.
Step 4: test rate and balance changes

Raising the rate to 6.75% on the same loan lifts the payment to $2,205.23 and total interest to $453,884.07. Adding $150 there shortens the term to 24 years 10 months and saves $92,077.26. A higher rate makes each extra dollar worth more, because it avoids more interest. To model a loan already in progress, balance and months remaining are enough. After 48 payments the balance here is $322,459.00 with 312 payments left. Entering that balance with 312 months and an extra $200 a month gives 254 further payments, which with the 48 already made is 302 in total, the same as running the whole loan with $200 extra starting at payment 49.
Step 5: pick the plan you can keep

A saving that you stop paying after a year is worth nothing. Rounding the payment up to $2,100, only $6.56 above the required amount, saves $4,511.29 of interest and ends the loan three months early. Choose an amount that fits your budget in a bad month, automate it, and re-run the calculator once a year.

items: Entering the original loan amount for a loan in progress. Use the current balance and the months remaining.
Not specifying that extra money goes to principal. Confirm with your lender how to label it and check the next statement.
Comparing runs that change several inputs at once. Change one thing per run.
Forgetting prepayment terms. Some loans, especially non-mortgage loans, may charge a fee or compute interest in ways that reduce the savings. Read the loan agreement.
Ignoring other uses of the money. Interest saved equals your loan rate, a certain return, but other uses such as an emergency fund or higher-rate debt may come first.

sections.text: When the calculator's answer will differ from your statement

The tool assumes a fixed rate, monthly interest on the remaining balance and payments made on schedule. Adjustable-rate loans, daily-interest loans, escrow changes, fees and skipped payments all move real figures. Use the results as a comparison between scenarios, which is where the calculator is most reliable, and treat your lender's statement as the authority on the exact balance.
